name: Passionflower / chamomile tea

lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is an herbal infusion drunk before bed for relaxation and sleep. Chamomile is the better known; passionflower is often blended in. People treat the wind-down and better sleep as support for rested skin and looks.

Both plants contain flavonoids such as apigenin, which proponents link to calming effects. Encyclopedic sources say there is no good clinical evidence for chamomile in insomnia, though its anti-anxiety potential is under preliminary research, and a 2013 review of passionflower reports a good safety profile. Combination products have been tested in at least one small registered trial.

paras: It is a cup or two of tea in the evening, brewed from dried flowers or tea bags, as part of a wind-down routine. It is often paired with other sleep habits.

Chamomile can cause allergic reactions, particularly in people sensitive to daisy-family plants, and may interact with some drugs. Passionflower may add to sedatives and anticoagulants. Pregnancy use is generally flagged for medical advice.

angle.text: People drink this traditional herbal tea before bed to unwind and sleep, a routine tied to rested skin and a fresher look. Reference sources describe limited clinical evidence for sleep; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is an herbal infusion drunk before bed for relaxation and sleep. Chamomile tea is made from the dried flowers of German chamomile or Roman chamomile [1], and passionflower (Passiflora incarnata, or maypop) is a plant whose dried aerial parts are listed in the European and British Pharmacopoeias [2].

Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence that chamomile treats any disease, that its anti-anxiety potential is under preliminary research, and that there is no good evidence for insomnia [1]. For passionflower, the 2013 review it cites reports a good safety profile [2]. Combination products have been tested in at least one small registered trial.
infobox: Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla or Chamaemelum nobile); Passiflora incarnata

paras: Chamomile flowers contain flavonoids and polyphenols including apigenin, quercetin and luteolin [1]. Passionflower contains flavonoids such as chrysin, apigenin, luteolin and quercetin, plus alkaloids, with the highest flavonoid concentration in the leaves [2].

A registered phase 1 trial (2019, 27 participants) tested a herbal formula, Rest-ZZZ, in healthy adults with difficulty falling or staying asleep [3]. No results are available in the sources reviewed. Studies of the teas themselves for sleep were not found in them.

Chamomile may interact with some herbs and drugs, may worsen pollen allergies, and can cause reactions in people allergic to daisies, ragweed and related plants; Roman chamomile may cause uterine contractions and is advised against in pregnancy [1]. Passionflower may increase the effect of sedatives, anticoagulants and MAO inhibitors, and pregnant or breastfeeding women are advised to consult a professional [2].
